text: These are shares of deaths, not risk. FARS counts deaths, not crossings or pedestrian-miles, so a large share says where deaths happen, not where a pedestrian is most likely to be killed.
This analysis is descriptive. It has no comparison with treated roads of the same class and traffic, so it does not estimate what any countermeasure would prevent.
2024 is the provisional Annual Report File: 13.7% fewer deaths than 2023 and 4.6% of them uncodable to the analysis population. Every 2024 figure will be re-read when the Final file is loaded.

The statewide list is right about the state and wrong about where each pattern lives: unlit high-speed arterial patterns are 1–3% of deaths in the five largest counties and 5–9% elsewhere. Check the county view before quoting a pattern.

Deaths with an unknown value stay in every denominator and no pattern contains an unknown. Speed is unknown for 6% of deaths, most of them hit-and-runs, so patterns with a speed item under-represent hit-and-run deaths.
The patterns describe urban, non-freeway roads only: 3,053 of 3,736 deaths. County rates use all deaths, so a rural county can have a high rate and contribute no pattern.
A rate or share built on fewer than 20 deaths is flagged unstable and is not ranked; one multi-victim crash can move it by several deaths.
Alcohol involvement is unknown for 44% of 2024 deaths, so no claim about impairment is made. Among the 253 deaths with no alcohol reported, all twenty combinations keep lift above one.

The speed and time-of-day bins were fixed in Week 6 from pooled single-variable frequencies that included 2024; the patterns measure joint structure, which that binning did not look at, but the contamination is disclosed.
